frontmatter.title: Time Series Analysis: Trends in Health Indicators and Gender Gaps (2000-2019)

children.value: This report examines temporal trends in health indicators and gender gaps across OECD countries from 2000 to 2019. By analyzing data across all years in this period, we can observe:
How gender gaps in Healthy Life Expectancy (HALE) and Life Expectancy (LE) have evolved over time
Trends in overall mortality rates (Mid values) for each health indicator
Trends in gender gaps (Gap values) for each health indicator
Which countries have shown the most improvement or deterioration in specific indicators
Which indicators show the strongest trends (increasing or decreasing) over the two-decade period
This temporal analysis complements the cross-sectional modeling approach by revealing dynamic patterns that may not be apparent in single-year snapshots. Understanding these trends helps identify:
Areas where progress has been made (narrowing gaps, declining rates)
Areas of concern (widening gaps, increasing rates)
Countries that serve as positive examples of improvement
Indicators with the strongest temporal trends that may require targeted interventions

: Cause-specific mortality indicators (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, neoplasms, alcohol use disorders, self-harm/suicide, interpersonal violence/homicide, road injuries, unintentional injuries, liver disease)
: Preserve all years from 2000-2019 (not just the most recent year)
: For each year, calculate the difference between male and female values
For predictors: Gap = Male - Female (positive gap means higher male rates)
For targets (HALE/LE): Gap = Female - Male (positive gap means women live longer)
: Average of male and female values, representing overall rates
: Focus on 38 OECD countries for consistency and data quality
For each indicator and country, we compute:
For each indicator, we identify countries with:
: Country with the highest average value over the period
: Country with the lowest average value over the period
: Country with the largest positive slope (most increasing trend)
: Country with the most negative slope (most decreasing trend)

The gap analysis complements the level analysis by highlighting gender equity dimensions
The HALE gap represents the difference in Healthy Life Expectancy between women and men (Female - Male, in years). A positive gap means women have longer healthy life expectancy.

children.alt: HALE Gender Gap Over Time (2000-2019) - All OECD Countries

children.value: HALE Gender Gap Over Time (2000-2019) - All OECD Countries
The figure above shows HALE gap trends for all OECD countries. Several patterns are evident:
: Gaps range from near zero (Netherlands, Switzerland) to over 6 years (Latvia, Lithuania)
: Most countries show relatively stable gaps over time, with gradual changes
: Some countries (notably in Northern Europe) have gaps close to zero, demonstrating that large gaps are not inevitable

The selected countries view highlights key examples:
: Consistently near-zero gap, showing that gender equity in healthy life expectancy is achievable
: Moderate gap (~3-4 years) with slight narrowing over time
: Large gaps (6-7 years) that have remained relatively stable
: Shows a gradual narrowing trend, suggesting overall improvement
The Life Expectancy gap represents the difference in overall Life Expectancy between women and men (Female - Male, in years).

Life Expectancy gaps show similar patterns to HALE gaps, but are generally larger (since they include years lived in poor health). The OECD average shows a gradual narrowing trend over the two-decade period.
The following tables show how HALE and Life Expectancy gaps changed for each country over the two-decade period:
: The majority of OECD countries have seen their gender gaps decrease from 2000 to 2019
: Changes range from substantial narrowing (>1 year) to slight widening
: Countries that narrowed HALE gaps also tended to narrow LE gaps
: Several countries (e.g., Netherlands, Switzerland) maintain or achieved near-zero gaps
